items.name: Mauretania & Roman Volubilis
items.description: Morocco's deep past includes Jebel Irhoud, where fossils around 300,000 years old are among the earliest known Homo sapiens. In the span shown here, Phoenician and Carthaginian traders founded coastal posts such as Lixus, and Amazigh (Berber) kings ruled the Kingdom of Mauretania — under Juba II it became a Roman client state. Rome annexed it as Mauretania Tingitana in 44 CE; Volubilis was its great inland city. Vandals crossed into North Africa in 429.

items.name: Idrisid Dynasty & Fez
items.description: Idris I, a descendant of the Prophet who fled the Abbasids, founded the first Moroccan Islamic state in 788 with Amazigh support. His dynasty developed Fez as its capital, and in 859 Fatima al-Fihri founded the al-Qarawiyyin mosque there, which grew into one of the world's oldest continuously operating places of learning.

items.name: Almoravid & Almohad Empires
items.description: Two Amazigh reform movements built empires spanning North Africa and al-Andalus. The Almoravids founded Marrakesh around 1070 and, under Yusuf ibn Tashfin, defeated Castile at Sagrajas (1086). The Almohads, inspired by Ibn Tumart, took Marrakesh in 1147, built the Koutoubia Mosque, and ruled from Spain to Tunisia until defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) began their decline.

items.name: Marinids, Wattasids & Saadis
items.description: The Marinids made Fez a showcase of madrasas and scholarship; the traveller Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier in 1304 under their rule. Portuguese seizures of coastal towns weakened the successor Wattasids. The Saadi dynasty, claiming descent from the Prophet, crushed a Portuguese invasion at the Battle of the Three Kings (1578), and Ahmad al-Mansur sent an army across the Sahara to conquer Songhai in 1591.

items.name: Alaouite Sultanate
items.description: The Alaouite dynasty, which still reigns, took Fez in 1666. Moulay Ismail (r. 1672–1727) built a grand capital at Meknes and a large standing army. Sultan Mohammed III was among the first rulers to recognise the United States, and the 1786 Moroccan–American treaty of friendship remains in force. In the 19th century, defeats by France at Isly (1844) and by Spain (1859–1860) exposed Morocco to growing European pressure.

items.name: French & Spanish Protectorates
items.description: The Treaty of Fez (1912) made most of Morocco a French protectorate, with Spain controlling the north and far south and Tangier becoming an international zone. In the Rif War (1921–1926), Abd el-Krim's forces routed Spain at Annual before a combined Franco-Spanish campaign defeated them. The nationalist Istiqlal party issued its independence manifesto in 1944; France's exile of Sultan Mohammed V in 1953 only strengthened the movement.

items.name: Independent Kingdom
items.description: Morocco regained independence from France in March 1956 and from Spain soon after. Hassan II (r. 1961–1999) consolidated royal power during the 'Years of Lead', a period of political repression later examined by the Equity and Reconciliation Commission (2004). The 1975 Green March asserted Morocco's claim to Western Sahara, whose status remains internationally disputed. Mohammed VI, king since 1999, oversaw a reformed family code (2004) and a new constitution (2011).
